P_41_DWPC: Among path methods, DWPC-LR was at least as accurate as DNFR on the three tasks with ten splits. On Hetionet drug repurposing DNFR minus DWPC-LR was +0.005 [−0.016, +0.025] (5/10 splits, inconclusive); on the two disease–symptom tasks DWPC-LR was ahead by 0.016 and 0.021, a difference under our rule on both. On PrimeKG DNFR was ahead by 0.070 [+0.056, +0.084] on two splits, too few for a verdict. Two controls separate the model from its training objective (Supplementary Table S23). Trained with DNFR's exact filtered softmax instead of sampled logistic regression, DWPC changed by +0.005 [+0.000, +0.008] on Hetionet disease–symptom (8/10 splits, equivalent), so the objective does not explain DNFR's deficit there. A linear model in the untransformed DWPC with non-negative coefficients, trained with the same softmax, reached 0.249 (+0.009 against DWPC-LR, inconclusive) and was ahead of DNFR by 0.025 [+0.019, +0.031] (10/10 splits, different); its optimum set 44% of the metapath coefficients to zero. On the graded graph, with one metapath, every increasing function of the single DWPC feature ranks the candidates identically, so all DWPC models gave DWPC-LR's MRR (0.331). We kept the damping of DWPC at 0.4, the value of Himmelstein et al. [1]; tuning it could only add to DWPC's accuracy. Degree and prior features did not help DWPC-LR. Completion of the target relation alone was far behind on Hetionet drug repurposing (Soft-Impute 0.262), came close on PrimeKG (0.627) and led on the dense graded graph (0.352 against 0.311 for DNFR), where a low-rank description should work well. AnyBURL was below DNFR and DWPC-LR wherever it ran<<ANYBURL_1000>>. The compact NBFNet, with about ten thousand parameters, did not differ from DNFR under our rule (graded graph −0.001 [−0.011, +0.009]; Hetionet disease–symptom +0.021 [+0.014, +0.029], ahead on 9 of 10 splits), and it was behind DWPC-LR on the graded graph (−0.022, different). Every path method was far above the chance level on every task.
P_44_PROFILE: Figure 2 shows the converged profiles with the disagreement between optimisation chains. The largest spreads in Supplementary Tables S8 and S16 (up to 32.1 × 10⁻³ nat on Hetionet) came mostly from single chains that settled in a poorer basin at every p, not from imprecision of the profile itself: on the graded graph the two best chains agreed within 0.08 × 10⁻³ nat at 46 of 48 grid points, and on Hetionet disease–symptom within 0.10 × 10⁻³ nat at 16 of 18 points on splits 0 and 2 (Supplementary Table S21). On these resolved profiles the training loss did locate p within a split, but loosely: on the graded graph the points within the threshold χ²(0.95, 1)/(2N) = 0.65 × 10⁻³ nat were [−0.5, −0.25] on split 1, {0.5} on split 2 and, on split 0, two disjoint ranges, p ≤ −2.5 and 0.1 to 0.25, separated by a ridge near p = −0.25 that rose 5.1 × 10⁻³ nat; on Hetionet they were [−20, −10] and [−5, −1]. On Hetionet split 1 the two best chains disagreed by 3 to 11 × 10⁻³ nat at 8 of 9 points, more than the profile varied, so that profile could not be resolved at the precision we attained. Across splits the minimiser moved (graded graph 0.1, −0.25 and 0.5; Hetionet −20 and −2), which is sampling variability of a weakly curved objective rather than flatness within a split. Profiles of the two metapaths that carry most of DNFR's evidence on Hetionet disease–symptom, with the other 15 re-fitted, were resolved (the two sweeps agreed within 0.01 × 10⁻³ nat at all but one cold-started point; Supplementary Table S22) and only one-sided: for disease–resembles–disease–presents–symptom (57% of the evidence) the loss rose by 2.6 × 10⁻³ nat from p = −5 to the product, the points within the threshold were [−5, −2], and validation MRR varied by 0.005; for disease–localizes–anatomy–localizes–disease–presents–symptom (33% of the evidence) the loss rose by 1.0 × 10⁻³ nat from p = −5 to the product, the points within the threshold were [−5, −0.5], and validation MRR varied by 0.001. The loss thus prefers operators towards the minimum for these metapaths without fixing a value, and held-out accuracy hardly distinguishes them.
P_44_HELDOUT: Held-out accuracy pointed elsewhere. On the graded graph, validation MRR at the converged fits peaked at p = −1.5, −2 and −1.5 (Figure 2C), where the training loss lay 1.2, 1.9 and 5.2 × 10⁻³ nat above its minimum, outside the threshold on every split; test MRR at the selected value exceeded that of the product by +0.014, +0.008 and +0.016. The data thus carry information about p that the training objective barely registers: the softmax loss averages over all candidates, whereas MRR depends on the order of the few top-ranked ones. This is a mismatch between the surrogate loss and the metric, not an absence of information, and it is why we profiled validation MRR, a ranking-aware criterion, beside the loss rather than a second likelihood. The Łukasiewicz t-norm, which lost 0.080 from the default initialisation because every path starts at strength zero, reached 0.312, 0.333 and 0.290 when started from the converged product (Supplementary Table S18). Per-metapath values from different starts were weakly correlated (median Spearman 0.44 on Hetionet disease–symptom), so learned per-metapath values should not be interpreted either.

P_46_FACTS: At the level of facts the picture is clearer. Summed path shares credited the leading fact with 45%, 25% and 28% of the evidence on the three tasks; its Shapley value was 16%, 12% and 9%, and half of the attribution lay on 7, 6 and 12 facts. The two criteria picked the same leading fact for 95%, 91% and 100% of pairs, so double counting changes how much a fact appears to carry more than which fact leads. Removing the leading fact from the graph left 85%, 60% and 76% of correct top-10 predictions in the top 10, against 100%, 99% and 99% for a random fact on the same paths. This counterfactual keeps degrees, and hence the memberships of neighbouring edges, fixed, as the Shapley decomposition does, and it measures how much the trained model depends on a fact, not what a model retrained without the fact would learn. DWPC-LR's counterfactuals were similarly faithful (87%, 55% and 82% against 100%, 99% and 96%), but its attribution is inexact and of mixed sign: on compound–treats–disease 31% of its positive attribution was offset by metapaths with negative coefficients (median). Both properties come from the asinh transform and the unconstrained coefficients, not from path counting. The linear non-negative DWPC model of Section 4.1 is a sum of non-negative path terms, each a unanimity game over its facts, so its edge-level Shapley value is exact and non-negative for the same reason as DNFR's. Its leading fact carried 8% of its attribution on Hetionet disease–symptom and half lay on 24 facts; removing its leading fact left 57% of its correct top-10 predictions in the top 10, against 99% for a random fact, and on the graded graph it coincides with DWPC-LR (Table 6). Exact, non-negative attribution to facts is therefore a property of additive path models with non-negative terms, not an advantage of fuzzy composition. On drug repurposing the leading metapath was associative for 100% of correct top-10 predictions (examples in Supplementary Table S19).
P_46_CLIN: In the pilot clinical assessment (Supplementary Sections S6.2, S7 and S8.7), the first rater judged every relation on a path to agree with biomedical knowledge for 53% [42–64%] of paths on Hetionet and 60% [49–70%] on the graded graph. The physician's usefulness ratings separated correct from incorrect predictions only weakly (AUC 0.67, 95% CI 0.49–0.83), and his agreement with the first rater on the correctness of relations was moderate (κ = 0.40, 0.23–0.57). The explanations were more often a reason to look further than a reason to believe.
P_51: Noisy-OR aggregation and hub discounting carried DNFR's gains over its ablations, with the same sign on every split of the three tasks with ten splits; a learned discount helped only with graded clinical evidence. The t-norm, the most visibly neuro-fuzzy part of the model, gave no consistent gain when learned. The training loss located its parameter only within wide or disjoint intervals, the location moved between splits, and it disagreed with the value that held-out accuracy preferred; validation selection helped where learning did not. As a predictor DNFR did not beat DWPC-LR on any task with ten splits, trailed completion on the graded graph and did not differ from a compact NBFNet, and the training objective did not explain its deficit against path counts. A linear path-count model with non-negative coefficients was more accurate than DNFR on Hetionet disease–symptom and has the same exact, non-negative attribution to facts. For accuracy and for exact attribution alike, then, simpler additive path models suffice on graphs like these; whether an exact fact-level attribution helps a clinician more than a metapath-level one is a question for a user study. On drug repurposing, paths through known indications carried almost all of the evidence on random splits, and when they were available in training they lowered accuracy for diseases without known treatments.
P_6: In a controlled component analysis on three medical link-prediction tasks with ten splits each, the accuracy of differentiable neuro-fuzzy path reasoning came from noisy-OR aggregation and hub discounting, and four plausible refinements did not improve it. The training loss constrained the t-norm parameter only loosely, its optimum moved between splits and differed from the one held-out accuracy preferred, so the operator should be selected on validation data and not interpreted when learned. Degree-weighted path counts were at least as accurate, and a non-negative linear version of them offers the same exact attribution to facts. On drug repurposing most of the evidence, for every path method, ran through known indications. Held-out compounds kept most of their accuracy through similar compounds, but held-out diseases did not, and for them a model trained without the target-relation metapaths was more than three times as accurate. For explainable clinical decision support, effort is better spent on how much each fact counts, how paths are combined, attribution to facts and tests of what the evidence rests on than on learning the operator that composes it.

S82: The two metapaths with the largest mean share of DNFR's evidence over its correct top-10 test predictions on split 0 of Hetionet disease–symptom were profiled one at a time (dnfr/profile_permp.py). With the parameter of the profiled metapath fixed, the other 15 parameters were free but kept in [−20, 0]: in a first attempt that allowed p up to 1, the free parameters of other metapaths drifted to the nilpotent range, where their paths reach strength zero and stop passing gradient, and the fits stalled at a higher loss. The other parameters ended at the product end of the range (median 0). The two profiles were fitted from separate cold starts and settle at losses about 6 × 10⁻³ nat apart, another sign that the full objective has several basins; within each profile the two sweeps agree to 10⁻⁵ nat except at the cold-started point. Both profiles fall monotonically towards p = −5 and stay within the threshold over a range of several units, while validation MRR varies by at most 0.005 (Table S22).
S83: Three DWPC models were added to DWPC-LR (dnfr/run_task.py, functions fit_linear_softmax and fit_nonneg_logistic). (i) The asinh-transformed features of DWPC-LR with a linear scorer trained by DNFR's exact filtered softmax over all candidate tails; pairs without paths score zero, which is exact because the intercept cancels within a query. (ii) A linear scorer in the untransformed DWPC, divided by the mean of each metapath as in DWPC-LR, with coefficients w = softplus(u) ≥ 0, trained by the same softmax. (iii) The same non-negative model trained with DWPC-LR's objective (20 sampled negatives per positive, balanced class weights). The L2 penalty of each was chosen from {10⁻⁴, 10⁻³, 10⁻², 10⁻¹} by validation MRR, and every model was fitted by L-BFGS. The score of model (ii) is a sum over paths of w_m w_π / mean_m with w_π ≥ 0 the degree-damped path weight; removing any fact of a path removes the path when degrees are held fixed, so each path term is a unanimity game over its facts and the Shapley value of a fact is exactly the sum of the terms of its paths divided by their lengths, as for DNFR (dnfr/explain_dwpc_nn.py). DWPC-LR was recomputed for the same splits and reproduced the released ranks exactly. The controls were run on the two disease–symptom tasks, as requested; on compound–treats–disease they were stopped for time.
S86: The rule of Section 3.6 applied to the validation-selected fixed p against the fixed product on the graded graph (Table 4, last row). The ten per-split differences in MRR were −0.005, +0.018, +0.023, +0.021, +0.023, +0.015, +0.025, +0.021, +0.029 and +0.025, with mean +0.0195 and 9 of 10 positive. The corrected resampled t-test [44], with test-to-training ratio 1/8, gave p = 0.0021; its 90% interval was [+0.011, +0.028] and its 95% interval [+0.009, +0.030]. The stratified paired bootstrap over test queries gave a 90% interval of [+0.015, +0.024] and a 95% interval of [+0.014, +0.025]. Equivalence requires both 90% intervals inside (−0.01, +0.01); neither is, so the comparison is not equivalent. The comparison belongs to the family of 14 refinement comparisons of this task; with the smallest p of the family, its Holm-adjusted p-value is 14 × 0.0021 = 0.030 < 0.05, and the 95% bootstrap interval excludes zero on the side of the mean difference, so the verdict is different (†).

P_45_TAIL: When every indication of a test disease was held out (Table 5A), the fixed product fell to 0.078 from 0.602 and DWPC-LR to 0.084 from 0.594 over 10 splits, and DNFR to 0.079 on the 4 splits on which it was run, about twice the chance level of 0.041. Completion, popularity and the edge prior (0.015, 0.010 and 0.013) fell to or below chance: every held-out disease has no training positive, so all of them tie at the bottom of a ranking by popularity. Degree and prior features hurt DWPC-LR (0.032 against 0.084). DNFR without degree terms reached 0.103 (+0.025 [+0.009, +0.041], 4/4 splits, inconclusive), a plausible reversal, since hubs are the diseases with many known treatments. Hits@10 separated the methods more than MRR did: at similar MRR, on the same four splits, the Hamacher product and DNFR without degree terms placed the true compound in the top 10 for 0.229 and 0.268 of test pairs, against 0.144 for DNFR. Because a clinician inspects a short list, Hits@10 is the more practical criterion here, but with about ten test diseases per split these differences are not established.
P_45_TREATS: On random splits, the 33 metapaths that contain the treats relation carried 99% of DNFR's evidence for its correct top-10 predictions, against 0.5% for metapaths through a gene that the compound targets. Without them (Table 5B), DNFR fell from 0.599 to 0.289 (−0.310 [−0.343, −0.277], different), DWPC-LR from 0.594 to 0.235 and the fixed product from 0.602 to 0.281. Removing the palliates metapaths too (Table 5C) changed DNFR by a further −0.012, and gene-only metapaths then carried 46.5% of its evidence. On the disease-centred split the picture reversed (Table 5D). Trained without the treats metapaths, the fixed product reached 0.273 and DWPC-LR 0.196 for held-out diseases, against 0.078 and 0.084 with them (+0.195 [+0.176, +0.215] and +0.113 [+0.097, +0.129], 10/10 and 10/10 splits, both different), close to their random-split accuracy without those metapaths (0.281 and 0.235) and about six times the chance level. With the treats metapaths available in training, both models presumably came to rest on known indications and gave little weight to the rest of the graph, which is all that a disease without indications has; without them, the same graph supported a useful zero-shot ranking. Known indications thus act as a shortcut that raises random-split accuracy and lowers accuracy for new diseases. When every indication of a test compound was held out instead (Table 5E, 10 splits), the fixed product reached 0.568 and DWPC-LR 0.555, against 0.210 for popularity and 0.041 for chance, far above the disease-centred level. A new compound loses its own indications but not those of similar compounds or compounds of its pharmacologic class, so this accuracy presumably still rests on the same association; we did not ablate the treats metapaths on this split. Random-split accuracy on curated drug repurposing thus comes largely from guilt by association, for DWPC-LR as much as for DNFR: a compound ranks high because similar compounds, or compounds of its pharmacologic class, treat the disease. The evidence outside the treats relation supports a lower random-split accuracy, but it is what carries over to a disease without known treatments, provided the model is trained on it alone.
